title: How to track webinar analytics: metrics, tools, and a step-by-step guide
summary: Learn how to track webinar analytics using key metrics, simple formulas, and a six-step process to review results and plan future events.
body_markdown:
The webinar's over, the chat has gone quiet, and the recording is processing. Many teams then ask: did it work? Webinar analytics can help teams review registration, attendance, viewing patterns, and audience interactions. This guide covers the metrics to consider at each stage, the formulas behind them, a six-step reporting process, and ways to use the results to inform a[post-event webinar strategy](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/post-event-webinar-strategy/) .

## What is webinar analytics?


Webinar analytics is the process of collecting and reviewing measures from stages of a webinar, including promotion, registration, the live session, and on-demand viewing, to assess results and inform future planning. It combines key performance indicators (KPIs), selected to assess an event's objectives, with engagement measures such as questions and poll participation.


A webinar can generate several measures, including registrations, live attendance, viewing duration, and audience interactions. Reviewing them together can help teams identify topics to consider when planning a future event.


## Webinar metrics to track before, during, and after your event


A useful way to organize webinar metrics is by attendee journey: registration before the event, attendance and engagement during it, and conversion and on-demand measures afterward. Reviewing each stage can help identify where additional analysis may be useful.


### Before the event: registration metrics


Start with the registration page conversion rate, which is the share of page visitors who register (registrants ÷ unique page visitors × 100). A lower rate may prompt a closer look at the page title, form length, and clarity of the takeaway.


Next, track registration source. Tagging each promotional link can help you compare channels with later attendance. Zoom's[guide to promoting a webinar](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/how-to-promote-a-webinar-your-pre-event-strategy-guide/) offers planning suggestions to consider when setting a promotion schedule.


### During the event: attendance and engagement metrics


Your webinar attendance rate is the percentage of registrants who join live (live attendees ÷ registrants × 100). It measures the share of registrants who attended; comparing it with reminder timing and event details may help identify factors to examine.


Average watch time, considered alongside the full session length, is one indicator of viewing behavior. A drop-off point can show where viewing declined, but does not by itself explain why. Engagement measures such as poll responses, questions submitted, chat messages, and reactions describe different forms of participation. An engagement rate can be calculated by adding selected interactions and dividing by the number of attendees; define the included interactions consistently.


Plan interaction prompts across the session. Zoom's[during-event strategy guide](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/how-to-run-a-webinar-your-during-event-strategy-guide/) offers examples of ways to invite participation.


### After the event: on-demand and pipeline metrics


The data keeps coming after the session ends. Track on-demand views and watch time for the recording, the click-through rate on your follow-up call to action (CTA clicks ÷ attendees × 100), and post-event survey responses.


For marketing and sales teams, one metric to consider is webinar-associated pipeline: the number of opportunities with a webinar touch and how those opportunities progress compared with others. This comparison describes an association; on its own, it does not establish that the webinar caused a deal outcome. Webinar ROI (return on investment) can compare a program's attributed value with its costs; define the attribution approach and costs consistently.


Here's a quick reference you can share with your team.


Metric What it tells you How to calculate it When to measure


Registration page conversion rate Share of unique page visitors who register Registrants ÷ unique page visitors × 100 During promotion


Registration source Channels associated with registrants Registrants grouped by UTM source During promotion


Webinar attendance rate Share of registrants who joined live Live attendees ÷ registrants × 100 After the live session


Average watch time Viewing duration considered alongside session length Total minutes watched ÷ attendees, compared with session length After the live session or recording period


Engagement rate Selected interactions per attendee (Poll responses + questions + chat messages) ÷ attendees After the live session


Follow-up CTA click-through rate Share of attendees who clicked the CTA CTA clicks ÷ attendees × 100 After the follow-up period


On-demand views Unique viewers of the recording Unique on-demand viewers Review periodically after publication


Webinar-associated opportunities Progression of opportunities with a webinar touch; association alone does not show causation Opportunities with a webinar touch ÷ total opportunities At regular reporting intervals


## How to track webinar analytics in 6 steps


To track webinar analytics, set a goal, tag promotional links, select engagement measures, review available reports, and compare results across sessions. Here's how each step works.


1. **Set one goal and choose three to five KPIs.** Decide what the webinar should move (new leads, product adoption, training completion) and pick the metrics that show whether it did. Clear goals make results easier to interpret and act on.
2. **Tag every promotional link with UTM parameters.** UTM (Urchin Tracking Module) parameters are short tags added to a URL that tell your analytics tools where a click came from. Use a consistent naming pattern for source, medium, and campaign so reports stay comparable across events.
3. **Plan engagement moments and capture them.** Put a poll early in the session, keep Q&A open, and add a mid-session CTA. Review aggregate interaction patterns as measures of participation; a single interaction does not establish an attendee's intent.
4. **Review available post-event reports promptly.** Consult the reporting options available to your team, and note anything unusual, such as a technical hiccup that may help explain a drop-off.
5. **Compare relevant reports.** Review webinar metrics alongside campaign or pipeline measures using your team's established reporting process. Describe observed relationships as associations unless supported evidence demonstrates causation.
6. **Review, compare, and improve.** Compare each session against your series average as well as your last event. If attendance dips, revisit timing and reminders. ## Using webinar metrics to inform future programs


Webinar metrics can inform planning for future events. Three practices can help structure the review.


**Compare attendance patterns.** Compare no-show rates across promotional channels or registration periods. Use any observed pattern to decide whether reminder timing or event messaging warrants a closer look. A follow-up message can point registrants to the recording.


**Track trends across a series.** Reviewing multiple webinars can provide more context than looking at a single event, though results may vary by topic and audience. Compare registration and participation patterns; treat any relationship with pipeline as an association unless a documented method supports a causal conclusion. Zoom's guide to[measuring webinar ROI](https://www.zoom.com/en/blog/measuring-webinar-roi-and-impact/) offers additional context for evaluating results.


**Give sales useful context.** Aggregate engagement themes, such as recurring questions or poll results, can inform follow-up planning. Avoid treating a single interaction as proof of an individual's intent.


Interpret total registrations alongside attendance and engagement measures; registration counts alone do not show how many people attended or participated.

## Frequently asked questions about webinar analytics


### How do you track webinar analytics?


To track webinar analytics, choose a goal and key performance indicators, tag registration links, and select engagement measures. After the event, review reports available to your team and compare results across sessions to identify patterns for further analysis.


### What webinar metrics should you track?


Commonly tracked webinar metrics include registration page conversion rate, webinar attendance rate, average watch time, engagement rate, and follow-up CTA click-through rate. Together, these measures can help describe registration, viewing, and follow-up behavior; no single measure proves why an outcome occurred. B2B teams may also track webinar-associated pipeline, while treating any observed relationship as an association unless a documented analysis supports a causal conclusion.


### How do you measure webinar ROI?


To estimate webinar ROI, compare the value attributed to a webinar program with its total costs, which may include software, promotion, and team time. One formula is (attributed value − cost) ÷ cost × 100. Use a consistent attribution method and consider reviewing results across multiple webinars rather than relying on a single event.


### Can you track webinar engagement in Zoom?


Check Zoom's current Webinars documentation for the engagement reports, data fields, and CSV export options available to your plan.


### How can you compare webinar metrics with business outcomes?


Compare webinar measures with campaign or pipeline results using a consistent method. Describe any observed relationship as an association unless documented analysis supports a causal conclusion. For current product reporting information, consult Zoom's official documentation.


## Start tracking what matters


You can begin tracking webinar analytics with a clear goal, consistent tagging, and a routine for reviewing results before a future event. Start with the measures in the table, interpret relationships carefully, and use findings to inform subsequent planning.
